title: Uniform Resource Identifiers (URI): Generic Syntax
summary: Defines the generic grammar of Uniform Resource Identifiers, the strings such as web addresses that name resources. It lets software split any URI into its common parts without knowing the details of each scheme. It was a draft standard, now replaced by RFC 3986.

eli5.summary: A web address is like a home address with a street, a number and a town. This document explains the rules for writing those addresses so every computer can read them the same way.

questions: what is the generic syntax of a uri
what is the difference between uri and url
what is the difference between a uri and a url
how does percent encoding work in a uri
subtitle: The generic grammar that lets software split any web address or other identifier into its common parts.

tldr.problem: Web addresses and other resource identifiers were defined piecemeal across several documents, so there was no single scheme-independent way to parse them or to resolve relative references.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2396 defines a generic URI syntax of scheme, authority, path and query, rules for escaping characters, and an algorithm that turns a relative reference into an absolute URI against a base URI.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2396 was a Draft Standard that revised and replaced the generic parts of RFC 1738 and RFC 1808. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 3986, and RFC 2732 updated it.

facts.label: Replaces
facts.value: Generic parts of RFC 1738 and RFC 1808

today: RFC 2396 is obsoleted by RFC 3986, which is the current generic URI syntax, and it was updated by RFC 2732. Its status was Draft Standard.

sections.title: What a URI Is
sections.content:
A Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) is a compact string of characters for identifying an abstract or physical resource. RFC 2396 defines the generic syntax, both absolute and relative forms, and revises and replaces the generic definitions in RFC 1738 and RFC 1808. Parts of RFC 1738 that defined individual URL schemes are excluded and left to separate documents.

A resource can be anything that has identity, from a document or an image to a service. It is the conceptual mapping, not the content at any one moment, so a resource can stay the same while its content changes. A URI can be a locator (URL), a name (URN), or both. A URL identifies a resource by its primary access mechanism, while a URN must stay globally unique and persistent even if the resource stops existing.

The grammar is a superset of all valid URI, so an implementation can parse the common components without knowing each scheme's rules. It is not a generative grammar for URI; each scheme's own specification does that.
sections.eli5: A URI is a name tag for anything you can point at, like a picture, a page or a weather report. The rules say how to write the tag so everyone can read it.

sections.title: Characters and Escaping
sections.content:
A URI is a sequence of characters, not octets, drawn from a small set chosen so it can be typed, read aloud or written on a napkin. The RFC calls this transcribability, and ranks it above having the most meaningful components.

Characters fall into classes. Reserved characters are ; / ? : @ & = + $ , and are used as delimiters. Unreserved characters are letters, digits and the marks _ . ! ~ * ' ( ) -. Data that has no unreserved representation is escaped as a percent sign followed by two hexadecimal digits, so %20 is a space. A literal percent must be written %25.

Escaping should happen only when a URI is built from its parts, and a URI must be split into components before escapes inside them are decoded. Implementers should avoid escaping or unescaping the same string twice. Control characters, space, < > # % " and the "unwise" characters { } | \ ^ [ ] ` are excluded and must be escaped when they occur as data.

The generic syntax has no way to say which character set a non-ASCII URI uses. An individual scheme may require one, set a default or provide a way to signal it.
sections.eli5: Only some letters and symbols are allowed in an address. For anything else, you write a percent sign and a short code, like using a secret code word for a space.

sections.title: The Four Components
sections.content:
An absolute URI is written <scheme>:<scheme-specific-part>. Hierarchical URI share a generic form with four main components: <scheme>://<authority><path>?<query>. Each except the scheme may be absent. URI that do not use the slash for hierarchy are treated as opaque by the generic parser.

The scheme starts with a letter and may contain letters, digits, +, . and the hyphen. Programs should treat upper case as equivalent to lower case, so HTTP and http match.

The authority follows // and ends at the next /, ? or the end of the URI. It is either a registry-based name or a server in the form userinfo@host:port. The host is a domain name or an IPv4 address, and literal IPv6 addresses are not supported. If the port is omitted, the scheme's default is assumed. Putting user:password in the userinfo is NOT RECOMMENDED.

The path is a series of segments separated by /, and a segment may carry parameters after a ;. A slash-separated path does not imply the resource is a file. The query is a string for the resource to interpret.
sections.eli5: An address has a kind (like http), a place (the website), a path to the exact spot, and sometimes a question tacked on the end. Think country, town, street and a note to the person at the door.

sections.title: References and Relative Resolution
sections.content:
A URI reference is what people actually write in documents. It may be absolute or relative, and may end with a crosshatch and a fragment identifier, as in page#part. The fragment is not part of the URI. It is interpreted by the user agent after retrieval, and its meaning depends on the media type of the result. A reference that is empty or holds only a fragment points into the current document and should not cause a new retrieval.

A relative reference omits a prefix and is meaningful only against a base URI. The base can come from, in order of precedence, the document content, the encapsulating entity, the URI used to retrieve the document, or an application-dependent default. In relative paths, the segments . and .. mean the current level and the level above.

The RFC gives an example algorithm in seven steps. It parses the reference, inherits the scheme and authority from the base when they are missing, merges the paths by dropping the base's last segment and removing ./ and segment/../ patterns, then recombines the components. Implementations need not use this algorithm, but their output can be tested against it. A reference with leftover leading .. segments is in error. A segment containing a colon cannot start a relative path unless it is written like ./this:that.
sections.eli5: If you tell a friend to go next door, that only makes sense if they know your house. A relative address works the same way: it starts from where you already are.

sections.title: Equivalence and Security
sections.content:
Different strings can name the same resource. When a scheme uses the common syntax, the scheme and host name are case insensitive, and an explicit default port is equivalent to no port. So http://www.XEROX.com equals http://www.xerox.com. Other rules are scheme dependent.

The RFC says a URI does not in itself pose a security threat, but there is no guarantee that a URL will keep locating the same resource. A URL with an unusual port can trick a client into talking to a different protocol; the RFC's example is a gopher URL used to cause a message to be sent via an SMTP server. Escaped delimiters such as CR and LF should not be unescaped before transmission. Putting a secret password in the userinfo is strongly disrecommended.
sections.eli5: Two spellings can point to the same place, like writing a name in capitals or small letters. And an address can be a trap, so be careful with strange door numbers and never put a secret password in one.

items.title: Reserved
items.text: ; / ? : @ & = + $ , used as delimiters; escape them when they are data.

items.title: Unreserved
items.text: Letters, digits and - _ . ! ~ * ' ( ) can appear as they are.

items.title: Escaped
items.text: A percent sign plus two hex digits, such as %20 for a space.

items.title: Excluded
items.text: Control characters, space, < > # % and the quote mark must be escaped.
